resources.string: The hour and the minute fill the screen, with the AM/PM marker where the clock reads in twelve hours, and nothing else: no seconds, no weekday, no date, no year, no month grid and no saying. This is what the app looked like on its first day; everything it grew since is still set where you left it and comes back the moment this is switched off.

Keep a margin clear of the screen edges

For a television that cuts off the edges of the picture. The clock moves in by a twentieth on every side, which is where the saying, the date line and the timer\'s bar live. Leave it off on a phone, and on any set made in the last ten years.

What a table clock does: the colon between the hour and the minute is lit for half a second and dark for the other half, exactly on the second. It applies only where the time is written on one line and so has a colon — a screen turned sideways, for instance. Where the hour and the minute are stacked there is no colon and nothing changes. The digits never move: the line is measured with its colon whether it is being painted or not.
Show the time as 12 hours, with AM and PM

Warning: did you know there is no settled agreement on how midnight and noon should be written, with AM and PM or in any other way? Different countries and different standards do it differently. A 12-hour clock brings confusion into communication, it can cause misunderstandings and disputes in contracts, and that can lead to loss and to accidents. If you want to use it anyway, please also decide below how midnight and noon should be shown — AM, PM, 0, NN, MN, or the 24-hour way.

How it is done elsewhere. Most clocks and phones: 12 PM at noon, 12 AM at midnight — which the United States\' own standards body calls ambiguous and advises against. The Philippines: 12 NN and 12 MN, which cannot be misread. Japan: the twelfth hour is written 0, so half past noon is 0:30 PM and midnight is 0:00 AM. Britain and the United States in writing: \"12 noon\" and \"12 midnight\" spelled out. Korea and China: the part of the day is named instead — daytime twelve, night twelve. Much of Europe and Latin America: the 24-hour clock for anything official, where 00:00 and 12:00 need no marker at all.

Seven in the evening reads 7:19 rather than 19:19. Where the hour and the minute are on one line, AM or PM sits small just after the minute, on the same baseline; where they are stacked, it takes a line of its own under the minute.

Tick which pages to carry. A settings file is plain text, one key to a line, in sections you can read and edit anywhere. A package is that same file with the fonts and pictures beside it, under fonts/ and img/ — what you want when the other phone has none of them.
Choose a file and it is read first, not applied: you see what is in it and tick what to bring in. A zip made here, a zip you built by hand, or a bare settings.ini all work.
Nothing in this file could be read as settings.

Brought in %1$d settings, %2$d files and %4$d layouts. %3$d names dropped, because what they pointed at is not here.
Let the clock wander, to spare the screen

Everything on screen drifts a few pixels at a time around a circle it takes hours to complete, so that no bright shape sits on the same pixels all day. It never leaves the margin, so nothing is clipped. Leave this on for a phone left showing the time — an OLED panel that has drawn the same numerals in the same place for months keeps them faintly forever. Turn it off if you would rather the clock held perfectly still; an LCD has nothing to burn in.
Off, the clock still reads in twelve hours but writes no marker at all — with the date and the calendar on screen as well as without them. The time takes the room the marker was keeping.
Use a country\'s way of writing it…
Most clocks and phones — AM, PM, 12:00 PM, 12:00 AM (the default)
The Philippines — AM, PM, 12:00 NN, 12:00 MN
Japan — 午前, 午後, 0:00 午後, 0:00 午前
China — 上午, 下午, 12:00 下午, 12:00 上午
Midnight as 00:00 — twelve-hour all day, except that

Each button shows how that number will be written; press it to turn it over. The hour and the day keep an answer for each form they are written in, because the conventions differ: a twelve-hour clock usually writes 8:05 where a twenty-four hour one writes 08:05, and Jul 5 is as ordinary as 07-05. So the hour button follows the clock above, and the day button follows the date format.

AM and PM are Latin abbreviations, and much of the world does not write them in Latin — 오전 and 오후, 午前 and 午後, or nothing at all. Write whatever you like here; nothing is checked. A long marker takes room from the time beside it, and a letter your chosen font has no glyph for comes out as a box. Leave one blank for the built-in AM, PM, NN or MN. Noon and midnight fall back to the after-noon and before-noon markers unless you give them their own, and the 00:00 reading stays bare whatever is typed.

AM means before midday and PM after it, so noon is neither — it is midday itself, and midnight belongs to two days at once. American standards go as far as calling 12 a.m. and 12 p.m. ambiguous. Every clock uses them anyway, and so does this one unless you say otherwise. NN and MN are the Philippine way and cannot be misread; the 0 hour is the Japanese one; and midnight can simply be written the 24-hour way. The choice applies to that hour only.
Take the colours from the system theme

Dark theme: white writing on black. Light theme: dark writing on white. The clock changes with the phone, without being restarted. Your own two colours are kept and come back the moment this is switched off.
This phone is in its dark theme, so the clock is white on black.
This phone is in its light theme, so the clock is dark on white.

This one is drawn rather than decided. Choose Automatic above to see the settings that steer the app\'s own arrangement; they are kept exactly as you left them.

Prepared for playing: %1$s. These hold frames ready to draw, so the clock never decodes a picture while it runs.
Keep the clock up, past the lock screen

The screen stays on, the lock screen does not cover the clock, and nothing takes it away — for a phone left showing the time, or running a timer. It already behaves this way when the charger starts it. Turn it on if you want to touch the clock: Android gives no touches to a screensaver or to anything over the lock screen, so the menu, the timer and the calendar all do nothing there.
ReteClock is not your screensaver yet.
Opens Android\'s own screensaver settings — it hides in a different place on every version. Pick ReteClock there, and choose when it should come on (while charging, or in a dock).
This phone has no screensaver settings screen.

Show the timer on the clock
Off, the clock is exactly as it was: no bar, no controls, and nothing extra drawn.

Every interval end also flashes the screen, whichever of these is chosen. On vibrate and on silent the timer says nothing aloud and plays none of your sounds. And whatever is chosen here, a phone switched to silent stays silent — on vibrate it will not sound, and on silent it will not buzz either.
This device has no speech engine, so an interval\'s message will not be spoken. Everything else — the beeps, the count into each ending, and the flash — works as usual.
This device\'s speech engine has no voice data installed, so a message will not be heard. Everything else — the beeps, the count into each ending, and the flash — works as usual.
This replaces every preset with the five the clock starts with — Pomodoro, Tabata, Tea, Ramen and Pasta. Presets you made, and changes you made to these, are lost.

One line per run: when it began, which timer, how many intervals it got through, how long it ran without the pauses, and the same starting moment as a Unix time. It is written on this phone only, and it goes when the app does.
A list of when you were here and what you were doing is personal information. It is off unless you turn it on, and the L on the timer strip is there so you can see when it is on.
At most %1$d MB; trim to %2$d MB
Whole megabytes. When the log passes the first number the oldest files are deleted until it is under the second. The most is 100 and 99; the least is 2 and 1.
The log could not be written out.
There is nothing in the log yet.
Delete everything the timer has written down? What is gone cannot be brought back.
Tap a preset to open its intervals. Each interval has its own colour, the colour it moves to as it runs, a message to speak when it begins, and a warning so many seconds before it ends.
Show a saying along the bottom
One a day, in a thin strip under the clock. Touch it for another. The sayings are from W. A. Clouston\'s "Book of Wise Sayings" (1893), which is in the public domain.
Clouston, W. A., comp. Book of Wise Sayings: Selected Largely from Eastern Sources. London: Hutchinson & Co., 1893. Public domain. Transcription: Project Gutenberg ebook 21130.

[Preston, Thomas], comp. A Dictionary of English Proverbs and Proverbial Phrases, with a Copious Index of Principal Words. London: Whittaker & Co., [n.d.]. The title page names neither author nor year; the attribution is Project Gutenberg\'s. Public domain. Transcription: Project Gutenberg ebook 39281.
Bohn, Henry G., comp. A Polyglot of Foreign Proverbs. London: Henry G. Bohn, 1857. Public domain. Transcription: Project Gutenberg ebook 51090.

All three were published before 1900 and their compilers are long dead, so the texts are in the public domain worldwide. Project Gutenberg\'s header, footer, licence and trademark have been removed, so no Project Gutenberg Licence attaches to anything in this app.

The calendar every date is counted in: the month under the time, the date beside it, and the screensaver. The names that ship are Latin letters and ordinary digits; rename any of them below. Every calendar here is right from 1900 to 2200; outside that the clock shows the Gregorian date.

Some of these calendars are read by people who spell their months differently — Cairo and the Coptic liturgy, Jakarta and Cairo again for the Hijri months, India\'s own spellings beside the scholarly ones. Neither is a correction of the other, so both are here.
Show the Gregorian date as a small badge
The Gregorian month and day, reversed out of a small box at the lower left of the date — 08.15. Only when another calendar is counting.
An Islamic month begins when the new crescent is seen, so the date differs between countries and communities. Set this once to match your own; it does nothing under any other calendar.
Iran and Israel begin the week on Saturday; much of the world on Monday.
The clock takes its time from

Android carries its own table of time zone rules, and on an old phone that table is frozen — so in every country that has changed or abolished summer time since, the phone is an hour out for part of the year. Setting the offset here goes round that: the clock asks the phone only what moment it is, and works out the rest itself.
In quarter hours, because the world uses them: India is +5:30, Nepal +5:45, the Chatham Islands +12:45.

Tap a month or a weekday to call it whatever you like. Nothing here is checked: any length, any alphabet, in your own language if you want it. What ships is three or four Latin letters because that is what fits the grid on a small old screen — past four characters the month grid can crowd and the date line can shrink, and a letter your chosen font has no glyph for comes out as a box. Leave one blank to get the built-in name back. These names belong to this calendar; each calendar keeps its own.

Both times are standard time — the clock you are on before summer time starts. A country that ends summer time at 02:00 on its summer clock ends it at 01:00 here, which is the same moment. If the start month is later than the end month, the period runs over the year end, which is what the southern hemisphere needs.
A rule, not a list of countries: it keeps working after the next country changes its mind, because it never claimed to know about that country.
If these differ, the one to trust is whichever matches your watch. Setting an offset here while the phone\'s own zone is also wrong will put the clock out twice over.

A month under the time, written in the clock\'s own text colour — and filled with the same picture, if the digits are.
On the clock, the arrows either side of the month page through it. It returns to this month whenever the clock is opened again.

Either way, a run that stopped answering opens this screen: that is how the app lets you undo a picture or a font that made the clock unusable.

The last run stopped answering, so the clock started without images, imported fonts, or a layout of your own — the app arranged it instead. A large animated GIF is the usual reason: remove it below, or untick BG, and start the clock again. Nothing was thrown away; the next healthy run has it all back.

Points are in seconds to one decimal, counted from the beginning of the file: 12.5 is twelve and a half seconds in. An end before the start means the whole file.
Bring in or take out a folder of sounds…
A whole folder of sounds travels in the same zip the fonts and pictures use, on the carry page.

Android\'s high-contrast text is switched on (Settings → Accessibility). While it is on, the phone draws a heavy outline around every word and throws away a picture used to fill writing — which is why text here, and in every other app, looks outlined. The clock itself works around it: it draws its own writing as shapes, so your picture still shows inside the digits and only the outline you asked for appears. Switch the accessibility setting off if you would rather have the plain rendering everywhere.
Bring in or take out a folder of pictures…
Pick several at once above, or carry a whole folder in one zip on the carry page — the same one the fonts and the sounds travel in.
This phone is on silent, so nothing will play — here or anywhere else in the app.

A bell rings while the clock is on screen — except while a timer is counting, which has the right of way: a bell falling then is passed over rather than queued. Touch the screen while one is ringing and it fades out and stops — that touch does nothing else. Nothing plays while the phone itself is on silent.
Choose at least one day, or this bell will never ring.

A chime of two or three seconds is easy to miss once and hard to miss three times over. Touching the screen while it is ringing fades it out and cancels the rest of the repeats, not only the pass that is playing.

0 means the bell only rings, as it always did. Any other number and the bell asks: ring again in that many minutes, or stop. It can only ask while the clock is on screen — the app is not running when it is not showing, so a bell put off is forgotten if you leave the clock. A timer counting at the moment it comes back around goes first, and the bell rings as soon as the timer is quiet.

Each of these can play one of your own sounds instead of the built-in beep. A message is still spoken where one is set — the sound and the message share the moment. Bring sounds in on the Sounds and bells page.

Show several layouts in turn: each row stays for its own time, then the next, and after the last the first again. Upright and sideways have their own lists, as they have their own layouts. While a list plays, the layout chosen on the Layout page shows only when it is switched off.
